phonemes.desc: Mu plus short epsilon — the name begins with a soft, warning sound.
Delta plus diphthong ου — the middle syllable that carries the hissing.
Sigma plus short alpha — the final hiss that ends the name like a snake's warning.

pronunciation.approximation: 'meh-DOO-sah' — the middle syllable is long and hissing; the name sounds like a warning.

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: μέδουσα (medousa), 'guardian, queen' — from the verb μέδεσθαι, 'to protect, to rule'

kin.label: PIE
kin.form: *med- 'to measure, to judge, to guard' — root of Greek μέδεσθαι and Latin mederi

kin.label: Gorgon
kin.form: One of the three Gorgons; her sisters are Stheno and Euryale

pronunciation.note: Médousa is Tier 2 because the Greek Μέδουσα preserves stress (acute on the short υ) but no long vowel. The name means 'Guardian' or 'Queen,' an ironic title for a figure whose gaze turns men to stone.

domains.title: The Gorgon
domains.subtitle: Petrification, Monsters, Death, and the Averted Gaze
domains.lead: Médousa is the most famous monster in Greek myth. Once a beautiful maiden, she was transformed by Athena into a creature whose gaze turns the living to stone. She is the horror of the seen that cannot be looked away from — and the power that heroes must confront indirectly.

cards.name: The Petrifying Gaze
cards.desc: To look directly at her is to become stone — the literal freezing of fear.

cards.name: Snake-Haired Horror
cards.desc: Her hair is a writhing mass of serpents, the uncanny made visible.

cards.name: The Decapitated Head
cards.desc: Perseus cut off her head; Athena placed it on her aegis as an apotropaic weapon.

cards.name: Birth from Blood
cards.desc: From her severed neck sprang Pegasus and Chrysaor — death producing wonder.

mythology.lead: Médousa's myth is unusual because it has a before and after. She was not always a monster. The story of her transformation makes her both victim and threat.

myths.title: From Maiden to Monster
myths.text: In Ovid's Metamorphoses (4.790–803), Médousa was a beautiful priestess of Athena in the temple at Sicyon. Poseidôn raped her there, and Athena, enraged at the desecration of her temple, transformed Médousa's beautiful hair into serpents. The earlier Greek sources (Hesiod, Theogony 270–283) present her as simply one of the Gorgons, daughters of Phorcys and Ceto, without the rape narrative. The Roman version makes her a tragic victim; the Greek version makes her an inherent horror.

myths.title: Perseus and the Head
myths.text: Perseus, sent by Polydectes to fetch the Gorgon's head, used Athena's polished shield as a mirror to approach Médousa without looking directly at her. While she slept, he struck off her head with a sickle given by Hermês. From her neck sprang Pegasus and the warrior Chrysaor. The beheading required divine tools and indirect vision: Médousa can only be defeated by not being seen.

myths.title: The Gorgoneion
myths.text: Perseus gave Médousa's head to Athena, who fixed it in the center of her aegis. The Gorgoneion became the most powerful apotropaic image in Greek art, warding off evil with the very power of the monster. It appears on shields, temple pediments, coins, and doorways throughout the Greek and Roman world. Death, once decapitated and controlled, becomes protection.

myths.title: From Horror to Beauty
myths.text: Archaic Greek art depicts Médousa as a grinning, tusked boar-like creature. By the fifth century BCE, sculptors — under Periclean classical influence — began to render her as a beautiful woman with serpent hair, culminating in the Rondanini Medusa and later Renaissance interpretations. The transformation of her image mirrors the Greek domestication of horror: what is terrifying must eventually be made comprehensible, even beautiful.

lore.syncretism: The Romans adopted Médousa directly, and her image proliferated on shields, mosaics, and architectural elements. In Neoplatonism she became a symbol of the material world that must be transcended — the petrifying gaze of illusion. Freud famously interpreted the Medusa head as a castration symbol, while feminist readings from Hélène Cixous onward have reclaimed her as a figure of female rage and the male fear of the female gaze. Her image persists in fashion, film, and psychology as the archetype of the dangerous woman.
lore.culturalLegacy: Médousa is the most visually recognizable monster in Western art. From Archaic gorgoneia to Caravaggio's Medusa to Versace's logo, her face sells protection, danger, and luxury. Psychologically, she represents the moment when desire turns to stone — the paralysis of fear. In feminist theory, she has become an emblem of the violence done to women and the rage that follows. Restoring Médousa restores the name of the figure who turns the gaze back on itself.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Médousa is the goddess of the averted gaze. She forces us to look indirectly, to use mirrors and shields, to approach truth without staring directly at it. This is not cowardice; it is wisdom. Some truths petrify.

The modern world stares at everything. We believe visibility is virtue and that looking is understanding. Médousa reminds us that some powers are defeated only by indirection, by reflection, by not making eye contact with horror. The restoration of her name is a small lesson in visual humility.

sources.name: Vernant, La mort dans les yeux

lore.archaeology: The earliest monumental Gorgon, the West Pediment of the Temple of Artemis at Corcyra (Corfu, ca. 580 BCE), shows Medousa in running-kneeling pose between panthers. Temples at Selinunte and Athens used gorgoneia as antefixes and akroteria. The Rondanini Medusa (Munich Glyptothek) and the Medusa Rondanini type preserve a late Classical severed head. Archaic coins from Paros, Neapolis, and Sicily spread the apotropaic Gorgoneion across the Greek world.
